questions.question: Design a parking lot system. Walk me through your approach.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to decompose a real-world system into cohesive classes and identify correct relationships (composition, inheritance, aggregation).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a single God class that does everything or missing key entities like ParkingTicket, leading to difficulty tracking vehicle entry/exit times.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention explicit concurrency handling for spot assignment and justify each design pattern choice with the specific problem it solves in this domain.

questions.direct_answer: A parking lot system needs ParkingLot (manages floors), ParkingFloor (manages spots), ParkingSpot (tracks occupancy), Vehicle hierarchy (Car, Motorcycle, Truck), ParkingTicket (entry/exit tracking), and FeeCalculator (pricing logic). Use Singleton for ParkingLot, Strategy for fee calculation, and Factory for vehicle creation.

items: ParkingLot: Singleton, holds List<ParkingFloor>, find spot, issue/process ticket
ParkingFloor: holds Map<String, ParkingSpot>, methods for available spots by type
ParkingSpot: spot ID, type enum, occupied flag, park/vacate methods
Vehicle: abstract class with licensePlate, VehicleType; Car/Motorcycle/Truck subclasses
ParkingTicket: generated on entry, tracks vehicle, spot, entry time
FeeCalculator: Strategy pattern for different pricing (hourly, flat)
DisplayBoard: Observer pattern to show availability

answer_sections.content: For a parking lot design, I start by identifying entities. The physical objects: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot. The actors: Vehicle (abstract) with Car, Motorcycle, Truck subclasses. The transactional objects: ParkingTicket issued on entry, Payment on exit. The services: FeeCalculator. ParkingLot is a Singleton since there's one. ParkingFloor has a map of spots keyed by spot ID for O(1) lookup. ParkingSpot tracks its occupancy and has a canPark() method that checks if the vehicle type fits. On entry: find available spot → park vehicle → issue ticket. On exit: calculate fee → process payment → free spot → mark ticket paid. FeeCalculator uses the Strategy pattern so I can swap in different pricing without changing ParkingLot.

follow_up_questions: How would you handle multiple parking lot locations?
How would you add support for electric vehicle charging spots?

sections.title: Breaking Down the Parking Lot System
sections.content: A parking lot design is about **entities** and **responsibilities**. Think of it like organizing a library: you need the building (ParkingLot), floors (ParkingFloor), shelves (ParkingSpot), books (Vehicle), and checkout slips (ParkingTicket). The **ParkingLot** acts as the entry point—it manages multiple floors and coordinates spot allocation. Each **ParkingFloor** holds a collection of spots and knows which are available. A **ParkingSpot** has a type (compact, large, handicapped) and tracks if it's occupied. **Vehicle** is abstract because cars, motorcycles, and trucks have different space needs—use inheritance here. The **ParkingTicket** is your contract: it records entry time, assigned spot, and vehicle details. Finally, **FeeCalculator** handles pricing—keep it separate so you can change billing rules without touching core parking logic. This separation of concerns makes the system maintainable and testable. Each class has one clear job, following the Single Responsibility Principle.

sections.title: Core Parking Lot Classes
Key Design Decisions
content: **Entity Identification**: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, ParkingTicket are the core nouns—each models a real-world concept with clear boundaries.
**Inheritance for Vehicle Types**: Abstract Vehicle class with Car, Motorcycle, Truck subclasses handles different size requirements through polymorphism.
**Records for Immutability**: ParkingTicket and ParkingSpot use records because their state shouldn't change after creation—prevents bugs from accidental mutation.
**Singleton for ParkingLot**: Only one physical parking lot exists in the system—Singleton ensures a single point of coordination and prevents duplicate state.
**Strategy for Fee Calculation**: FeeCalculator interface allows swapping hourly, flat-rate, or vehicle-type pricing without changing ParkingLot code.
**Composition over Inheritance**: ParkingLot HAS-A list of floors, ParkingFloor HAS-A list of spots—models real containment relationships correctly.
**Optional for Spot Search**: findAvailableSpot returns Optional<ParkingSpot> to explicitly handle the no-spot-available case without null checks.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd design this system around five core entities. First, the ParkingLot itself—it's the entry point that manages multiple floors and coordinates vehicle parking. I'd make it a Singleton because there's only one physical lot in the system. Each ParkingFloor contains a collection of ParkingSpots and knows how to find available ones. The ParkingSpot tracks whether it's occupied and what type it is—compact, large, or handicapped. For vehicles, I'd use an abstract Vehicle class with subclasses for Car, Motorcycle, and Truck. This lets me handle different size requirements through polymorphism—a truck might need two spots while a motorcycle needs one. The ParkingTicket is crucial—it records entry time, assigned spot, and vehicle details. Without it, you can't calculate fees or track how long a vehicle has been parked. For fee calculation, I'd use the Strategy pattern with a FeeCalculator interface. This lets you plug in different pricing models—hourly, flat rate, or based on vehicle type—without touching the core parking logic. One pitfall freshers hit is forgetting about concurrency. If two cars try to grab the same spot simultaneously, you need synchronized methods or locks on the spot assignment operation. The key is separating concerns: each class has one job, and they communicate through well-defined interfaces. That's what makes the design maintainable.

questions.question: How does the fee calculation work in your parking lot design?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Strategy pattern and ability to isolate business logic that changes frequently from stable system structure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hardcoding fee calculation directly in ParkingLot or ParkingTicket classes, making it impossible to change pricing rules without modifying core code.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how Strategy enables A/B testing different pricing models in production by simply swapping the calculator instance at runtime.

questions.direct_answer: Fee calculation uses the Strategy pattern. Define a FeeCalculator interface with calculateFee(ParkingTicket ticket) method. Concrete implementations like HourlyFeeCalculator, FlatRateFeeCalculator, and VehicleTypeFeeCalculator contain the pricing logic. ParkingLot holds a FeeCalculator reference and delegates fee computation to it.

answer_sections.content: For fee calculation, I use the Strategy pattern. I define a FeeCalculator interface with a single calculate() method that takes a ParkingTicket (which has entry time, vehicle type, spot type). HourlyFeeCalculator multiplies hours parked by the hourly rate for that vehicle type. FlatRateFeeCalculator returns a flat fee. WeekendPricingCalculator might apply different rates on weekends. ParkingLot holds a FeeCalculator reference — at runtime, you can swap the strategy without changing ParkingLot code. This aligns with OCP: adding a new pricing model means adding a new class, not modifying existing ones. BigDecimal for money — never float or double for currency calculations.

follow_up_questions: Why do you use BigDecimal instead of double for fee calculations?
How would you handle free parking for the first 30 minutes?

sections.title: Strategy Pattern for Flexible Pricing
sections.content: Fee calculation is business logic that **changes frequently**—hourly rates adjust, weekend discounts appear, or you introduce surge pricing. You don't want this volatility infecting your core parking classes. The **Strategy pattern** solves this by extracting the algorithm into its own interface. Think of it like payment methods at checkout: whether you pay with cash, card, or digital wallet, the checkout process stays the same—only the payment mechanism changes. Here, **FeeCalculator** is the interface, and each concrete implementation (HourlyFeeCalculator, FlatRateFeeCalculator) encapsulates one pricing strategy. The **ParkingLot** holds a reference to a FeeCalculator and delegates all fee computation to it. This decouples the parking logic from pricing logic. When business wants a new pricing model, you write a new calculator class—no changes to ParkingLot, ParkingTicket, or any other entity. The ticket just carries data (entry time, exit time, vehicle type), and the calculator interprets that data according to its rules. This makes testing easier too: you can unit test each pricing strategy in isolation.

sections.title: Strategy Pattern Implementation for Fees
Key Design Benefits
content: **Open/Closed Principle**: Add new pricing models by creating new FeeCalculator implementations without modifying existing ParkingLot or ParkingTicket code.
**Single Responsibility**: ParkingLot manages parking operations, FeeCalculator handles pricing—each class has one reason to change.
**Runtime Flexibility**: Swap fee calculation strategies at runtime using setFeeCalculator, enabling A/B testing or time-based pricing (weekday vs weekend rates).
**Testability**: Unit test each calculator in isolation with mock ParkingTicket objects—no need to spin up the entire parking system.
**Composition over Inheritance**: ParkingLot HAS-A FeeCalculator rather than subclassing for different pricing modes, avoiding rigid class hierarchies.
**Interface Segregation**: FeeCalculator has one method—clients only depend on what they use, and implementations aren't burdened with unused methods.
**Immutable Ticket Data**: ParkingTicket is a record carrying immutable data—calculators read it but can't modify it, preventing side effects.

sections.title: How to Explain Fee Calculation Design
sections.content: I'd use the Strategy pattern for fee calculation because pricing rules change frequently—you might start with hourly rates, then add weekend discounts, or introduce surge pricing during peak hours. You don't want those changes rippling through your entire codebase. So I'd create a FeeCalculator interface with one method: calculateFee that takes a ParkingTicket and returns a BigDecimal. Then I'd write concrete implementations for each pricing model. HourlyFeeCalculator multiplies the hourly rate by the duration the vehicle was parked. FlatRateFeeCalculator just returns a fixed amount regardless of time—useful for events or monthly passes. VehicleTypeFeeCalculator charges different rates based on whether it's a motorcycle, car, or truck. The ParkingLot class holds a reference to a FeeCalculator and delegates all fee computation to it. This decouples parking operations from pricing logic. When business wants a new pricing model, I just write a new calculator class—no changes to ParkingLot, no changes to ParkingTicket. The ticket itself is just data: entry time, exit time, vehicle type. The calculator interprets that data according to its rules. You can even swap calculators at runtime using a setter method, which lets you do things like switch to weekend pricing on Saturdays or run A/B tests on pricing strategies. The key benefit is the Open/Closed Principle: the system is open for extension—add new strategies—but closed for modification—core classes don't change.

questions.question: How would you extend the parking lot design for multiple locations?

interviewer_intent.testing: Extensibility thinking—can the candidate evolve a design to handle new requirements without breaking existing abstractions or creating tight coupling.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to retrofit ParkingLot as a multi-location entity, violating Single Responsibility Principle and creating a tangled design.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss how the network layer could use the Composite pattern to treat single lots and lot collections uniformly, enabling recursive aggregation.

questions.direct_answer: Introduce a ParkingLotNetwork or ParkingManagementSystem class that aggregates multiple ParkingLot instances. Each ParkingLot remains an independent unit with its own floors and spots. The network layer provides cross-location operations like findNearestAvailableSpot(Location userLocation) or getTotalOccupancyAcrossAllLots().

answer_sections.content: If there are multiple locations, I introduce a ParkingLotNetwork class. Each ParkingLot is still a complete, independent unit. ParkingLotNetwork holds a List<ParkingLot> and has methods like findNearestLotWithAvailability(Location, VehicleType). This doesn't require changing the existing ParkingLot class at all — OCP in action. For cross-lot operations, ParkingLotNetwork can aggregate availability across all lots or route vehicles to the best option based on proximity. I'd also extract an IParkingLot interface that both ParkingLot and ParkingLotNetwork implement — then calling code works with either one. This follows the Composite design pattern — individual lots and the network both implement the same interface.

follow_up_questions: What design pattern are you applying when ParkingLotNetwork and ParkingLot share an interface?
How would you implement a 'find nearest lot' algorithm?

sections.title: Evolving the Design for Scale
sections.content: When requirements change—supporting multiple parking lot locations—the worst thing you can do is **retrofit** your existing ParkingLot class to handle this. That violates the Single Responsibility Principle: ParkingLot should manage one physical lot, not a network. Instead, introduce a new abstraction layer. Think of it like a retail chain: each store operates independently, but corporate headquarters coordinates across all stores. Here, **ParkingLotNetwork** (or ParkingManagementSystem) is headquarters—it holds a collection of ParkingLot instances and provides network-level operations. Each **ParkingLot** remains unchanged: it still manages its own floors, spots, and tickets. The network layer adds new capabilities: find the nearest lot with available spots, get total occupancy across all locations, or route users to the least crowded facility. This **layered approach** preserves your existing design. Old code continues to work—tests don't break, behavior doesn't change. You're extending functionality by adding new classes, not modifying old ones (Open/Closed Principle). The network coordinates, individual lots execute. This separation also mirrors real organizational structure: local managers run each lot, regional managers oversee the network.

sections.title: Network Layer for Multiple Locations
Extensibility Principles Applied
content: **New Abstraction Layer**: ParkingLotNetwork manages cross-location concerns while ParkingLot remains focused on single-location operations—maintains Single Responsibility.
**Open/Closed Principle**: Existing ParkingLot code doesn't change—you extend functionality by adding the network layer, not modifying core classes.
**Location as First-Class Entity**: Introduce a Location record with latitude and longitude—enables geographic operations like distance calculation and routing.
**Aggregation not Inheritance**: Network HAS-A collection of lots, not IS-A specialized lot—models the real-world relationship correctly without forcing a hierarchy.
**Composite Pattern Potential**: Treat single lots and lot networks uniformly by making both implement a common interface—enables recursive composition for franchise hierarchies.
**Stream API for Aggregation**: Use Java streams to compute network-level metrics like total occupancy or nearest lot—functional approach keeps code concise.
**Backward Compatibility**: Existing code using ParkingLot continues to work unchanged—tests pass, behavior preserved, no regression risk.

sections.title: How to Discuss Design Extension
sections.content: When extending to multiple locations, the key principle is don't break what already works. The existing ParkingLot class is designed for one physical location—it manages floors, spots, and tickets. If you try to make it handle multiple locations, you violate Single Responsibility and create a mess. Instead, I'd introduce a new abstraction layer: ParkingLotNetwork. This class aggregates multiple ParkingLot instances, treating each as an independent unit. Each lot still operates the same way—nothing changes in its internal logic. The network layer adds cross-location operations. For example, findNearestAvailableLot takes the user's location and searches across all lots, computing distance and filtering for availability. getTotalOccupancy sums occupied spots across all locations. These are network-level concerns, not individual lot concerns, so they belong in a separate class. To make this work, each ParkingLot now needs a Location—a record with latitude and longitude. This enables distance calculations. The network holds a Map of lotId to ParkingLot, making lookups efficient. You could even use the Composite pattern here: define a ParkingFacility interface that both ParkingLot and ParkingLotNetwork implement. That way, you can treat a single lot and a network of lots uniformly—useful if you have franchises or regional hierarchies. The beauty of this approach is extensibility. Existing code doesn't change—tests pass, behavior is preserved. You're adding new functionality on top, not retrofitting old classes. That's the Open/Closed Principle in action: open for extension, closed for modification.

questions.question: What design patterns did you apply in the parking lot design and why?

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of design pattern knowledge and ability to justify pattern choices with concrete benefits specific to the parking lot domain.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing patterns without explaining why they're needed or applying them where simpler solutions would suffice, showing pattern obsession over pragmatism.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast each pattern with the problem it solves—explain what would break or become unmaintainable without the pattern.

questions.direct_answer: Singleton ensures one ParkingLot instance system-wide. Strategy decouples fee calculation from parking logic, allowing runtime swaps. Observer updates DisplayBoards when spot status changes without tight coupling. Factory Method creates Vehicle subclasses, centralizing instantiation. Builder constructs complex ParkingTicket objects with optional fields cleanly.

answer_sections.content: I applied several patterns deliberately. Singleton for ParkingLot — there's one, and having multiple instances would be a bug. Strategy for FeeCalculator — pricing rules change without requiring changes to ParkingLot. Observer for the DisplayBoard — when a ParkingSpot's occupancy changes, it notifies the DisplayBoard to update availability counts; this decouples spot management from display. Factory Method for Vehicle creation — VehicleFactory.create(VehicleType.CAR) returns the right subclass without the caller knowing the exact type. Builder for ParkingTicket — it has many optional fields (entryTime, vehicle, spot, status) and Builder makes construction readable. Each pattern was applied to solve a specific design problem, not just to use patterns.

sections.title: Patterns as Problem Solvers
sections.content: Design patterns aren't decorations—they solve **specific problems** in your design. In a parking lot system, patterns emerge naturally from requirements. **Singleton** for ParkingLot: there's one physical lot, and having multiple instances would create state synchronization nightmares—two instances could assign the same spot twice. **Strategy** for fee calculation: pricing rules change frequently (hourly, flat rate, surge pricing), and you can't hardcode them in ParkingLot without making every price change a code deployment. **Observer** for display boards: when a spot's status changes, multiple display boards need updates—Observer lets them subscribe to changes without the spot knowing about displays, avoiding tight coupling. **Factory Method** for vehicle creation: you're parsing vehicle types from input (license plate, type string) and need to instantiate Car, Motorcycle, or Truck—Factory centralizes this logic and handles invalid types gracefully. **Builder** for ParkingTicket: tickets have many fields (vehicle, spot, entry time, exit time, fee, payment status), some optional—Builder makes construction readable and prevents telescoping constructors. Each pattern addresses a real pain point. The key is articulating **what breaks without the pattern**.

sections.title: Patterns in Action
Pattern Justifications
content: **Singleton for ParkingLot**: Prevents multiple instances from managing the same physical resource—two instances could double-assign spots, causing state inconsistency.
**Strategy for FeeCalculator**: Enables runtime pricing changes without code modifications—switch from hourly to flat-rate by swapping calculator instances.
**Observer for DisplayBoards**: Decouples ParkingSpot from display logic—spots notify observers of changes without knowing who's listening or how they react.
**Factory Method for Vehicles**: Centralizes instantiation logic and error handling—client code doesn't need switch statements or type checks scattered everywhere.
**Builder for ParkingTicket**: Avoids telescoping constructors with 8+ parameters—makes ticket creation readable and allows optional fields without overloading constructors.
**Without Singleton**: Multiple ParkingLot instances lead to race conditions on spot assignment and inconsistent views of lot occupancy.
**Without Strategy**: Every pricing change requires modifying ParkingLot code, recompiling, and redeploying—violates Open/Closed Principle and increases defect risk.

sections.title: Articulating Pattern Choices
sections.content: I'd use five key patterns in this design. First, Singleton for the ParkingLot class. There's one physical parking lot in the system, and having multiple instances would create chaos—two instances could assign the same spot to different cars, or they'd have conflicting views of occupancy. Singleton ensures a single source of truth. I'd use double-checked locking for thread safety. Second, Strategy for fee calculation. Pricing rules change constantly—you start with hourly rates, then add weekend discounts, then surge pricing during events. If you hardcode that in ParkingLot, every pricing change requires modifying core code. With Strategy, I define a FeeCalculator interface and plug in different implementations: HourlyFeeCalculator, FlatRateFeeCalculator, whatever business needs. You can even swap them at runtime. Third, Observer for display boards. When a spot's occupancy changes, multiple displays need updates—entrance boards, floor displays, mobile apps. Observer lets them subscribe to spot changes. The spot just notifies its observers—it doesn't know what they do or even how many there are. This decouples parking logic from UI concerns. Fourth, Factory Method for vehicle creation. You're parsing input—license plate and vehicle type as a string—and you need to instantiate the right subclass: Car, Motorcycle, or Truck. Factory centralizes this with a createVehicle method that takes the type string and returns the correct object. It also handles invalid types cleanly without scattering error handling. Fifth, Builder for ParkingTicket construction. Tickets have many fields: vehicle, spot, entry time, exit time, fee, payment status. Some are optional. Without Builder, you'd have telescoping constructors with eight parameters, and it's unclear which is which. Builder makes it readable: new ParkingTicket dot Builder dot vehicle dot spot dot build. Each pattern solves a real problem. The key in interviews is explaining what breaks without the pattern.

questions.question: How would you handle concurrent access to parking spots in your design?

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of concurrency issues in production systems and knowledge of Java threading primitives to prevent race conditions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Ignoring concurrency entirely or applying overly coarse locks (synchronizing entire ParkingLot) that kill throughput and create bottlenecks.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss lock granularity trade-offs—fine-grained locks on individual spots vs coarse locks on floors—and mention lock-free alternatives like compareAndSet for spot status.

questions.direct_answer: The critical section is check-and-occupy of a spot—two threads could both see a spot as available and try to occupy it simultaneously. Use synchronized on the parkVehicle method or ReentrantLock around the spot assignment operation. ConcurrentHashMap for spot lookups prevents iteration issues during updates. Atomic operations on spot status prevent partial state visibility.

answer_sections.content: Concurrency is a real concern in a parking lot system — multiple entry barriers could assign the same spot simultaneously. The race condition is the classic check-then-act: both threads see occupied=false, both park, both think they succeeded. The fix: make the check-and-set atomic. I'd make tryPark() synchronized on the ParkingSpot, or better, use AtomicBoolean for the occupied flag and compareAndSet() for lock-free thread safety. The ParkingFloor's spot lookup also needs to be thread-safe — use ConcurrentHashMap instead of HashMap. For the interview, acknowledging this issue and describing the solution demonstrates production thinking, even if we're designing at the class level.

follow_up_questions: What is a race condition and why does it happen in this parking lot scenario?
When would you use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized?

beats.text: AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) atomically checks the current value and sets it — if two threads race, only one gets true back. The other gets false and must find a different spot.

production trap: don't synchronize at the ParkingLot level — that serializes all spot assignments across all floors, which kills throughput. Synchronize at the individual ParkingSpot level so different spots can be assigned concurrently.

sections.title: Race Conditions in Spot Assignment
sections.content: Concurrency is the hidden killer in parking lot designs. Imagine two cars arriving at the same millisecond, both querying for an available spot. Without synchronization, both threads could execute the check-and-occupy sequence simultaneously: Thread A reads spot 42 as available, Thread B reads spot 42 as available, Thread A marks it occupied, Thread B overwrites and marks it occupied—now two cars think they own the same spot, leading to a physical conflict when they arrive. This is a **race condition**: the outcome depends on unpredictable thread scheduling. The **critical section** is the atomic check-and-occupy operation—checking availability and marking occupancy must happen together, indivisibly. In Java, you have several tools: **synchronized** methods or blocks for mutual exclusion, **ReentrantLock** for more control (try-lock with timeout, fairness), **ConcurrentHashMap** for thread-safe collections without external locking, and **AtomicBoolean** for lock-free status updates. The key trade-off is **lock granularity**. A coarse lock (synchronize the entire parkVehicle method) is simple but kills throughput—only one car can park at a time across all floors. A fine-grained lock (one lock per spot or per floor) allows parallelism but increases complexity and risk of deadlocks if not careful. For freshers, start simple: synchronized, then discuss optimizations.

sections.title: Thread-Safe Spot Assignment
Concurrency Strategies
content: **Critical Section**: The check-and-occupy sequence on a spot must be atomic—separate threads can't interleave between checking availability and marking occupancy.
**Synchronized Methods**: Simplest approach—synchronized parkVehicle ensures mutual exclusion but limits throughput to one parking operation system-wide.
**ReentrantLock per Spot**: Fine-grained locks allow multiple cars to park simultaneously on different floors—improves parallelism but increases code complexity.
**Volatile Keyword**: Ensures isOccupied changes are immediately visible to all threads—prevents caching issues where one thread sees stale availability data.
**ConcurrentHashMap**: Thread-safe map for spot collections—allows concurrent reads and controlled concurrent writes without external synchronization.
**AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet**: Lock-free atomic operation—checks current value and updates only if unchanged, preventing race conditions without locks.
**Lock Granularity Trade-off**: Coarse locks are simpler but reduce throughput; fine-grained locks enable parallelism but risk deadlocks and increase complexity.

sections.title: Discussing Thread Safety in Interviews
sections.content: Concurrent access is a real concern in production parking lot systems because multiple users are trying to park simultaneously. The critical problem is a race condition during spot assignment. Imagine two cars arriving at the same time. Both threads query for available spots, and both see spot 42 as free. Then both try to occupy it—depending on thread scheduling, both might succeed, and now two cars think they own the same spot. That's a disaster in the real world. The critical section is the check-and-occupy operation. Checking if a spot is available and marking it occupied must happen atomically—no other thread can interleave between those two steps. The simplest solution is to make the parkVehicle method synchronized. This ensures only one thread can execute it at a time, so spot assignment is sequential. The downside is throughput: even if you have ten floors with hundreds of spots, only one car can park at a time across the entire lot. That's overly conservative. A better approach is fine-grained locking. Each ParkingSpot gets its own ReentrantLock. When a thread tries to occupy a spot, it calls tryOccupy, which attempts to acquire the spot's lock. Inside the lock, it double-checks availability and marks it occupied. This allows multiple cars to park simultaneously as long as they're targeting different spots. You can also use ConcurrentHashMap for the spot collection—it's thread-safe and allows concurrent reads without locking. For even better performance, you can use AtomicBoolean for the occupancy flag with compareAndSet. This is lock-free: it atomically checks if the spot is available and marks it occupied in one CPU instruction, avoiding lock contention entirely. The key trade-off is simplicity versus throughput. For a fresher interview, I'd start with synchronized to show I understand the race condition, then mention fine-grained locks or atomic operations as optimizations for high-throughput scenarios.
